the loss of neuroprotective helper and regulatory T cells in the peripheral blood and the affected areas of the spinal cord is associated with the progression of ALS.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the observed increase in the proportion of CD4+, and a simultaneous decrease in the percentage of CD4+, CD25+ cells, in the peripheral blood might be a reflection of a neuroprotective response in the early phase, and a subsequent neurodegenerative response in the later stages of the disease.

the higher CD4+ T cell count in peripheral blood of ALS patients might be a sign of early disease onset and the reduced number of regulatory T cells might be an early sign of progression to later disease phases.
the loss of CD4+ CD25+ Treg lymphocytes and FOXP3 and CD25 gene expression in the peripheral blood is a potential biomarker for ALS progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD4+ helper and CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T lymphocytes might play a role as a prognostic marker in ALS.
the loss of CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T lymphocytes is an early event in ALS pathogenesis and might be a good marker for the prediction of disease progression.
the count of CD25+ Treg and the level of FOXP3 gene expressions in PBMCs of patients with ALS can be used as a prognostic biomarker of ALS.
